title: The diamond vehicle, deeper
hookLine: the Vajrayana builds on the Mahayana with tantra, ritual and a close bond with a teacher

lines: THE VAJRA NAMES A WHOLE WAY.
cards: On a low table in a Tibetan shrine room sit two small objects. One is a short metal scepter, pinched in the middle and flaring out at both ends like two closed flowers. The other is a hand bell.
A practitioner picks up the scepter in the right hand and the bell in the left, crosses the wrists, and rings. The scepter is called a vajra, and it gives a whole way of Buddhism its name.

teach.b: First, what it builds on. You walked a little way down this path in year one; now, further in. The Vajrayana doesn't throw out what came before.
Its aim is the Mahayana aim: to wake up for the sake of all beings. Bodhicitta, compassion and emptiness all stay underneath, Tibetan teachers say. What changes is the method.

Vajra is usually rendered as diamond, or thunderbolt: something that can't be broken, and something that strikes fast. So the diamond vehicle presents itself as a strong, quick way to the same awakening. Second, tantra.

The word names a family of texts and the practices they teach: mantra, the sacred sound, like Om mani padme hum from year one; mandala, the sacred map, like the sand mandala swept into the river; and visualization, where a practitioner pictures a buddha or a figure like Tara so clearly that, in the teaching, the line between seer and seen begins to soften.

teach.h: BODY, SPEECH AND MIND AT WORK.
teach.b: Body, speech and mind are all put to work: the hands hold the vajra and the bell, or make gestures called mudras; the voice chants; the mind holds the image. Nothing about a person is left out of practice.

teach.h: A CLOSE BOND WITH A TEACHER.
teach.b: In the Vajrayana the bond with a teacher, a lama or guru, is close and central.
Teachings are given in person, often through an empowerment, a ceremony that opens a practice to the student.

That's why Tibetan teachers themselves warn students to check a teacher carefully, for a long time, before trusting. The bell in the left hand, the vajra in the right: wisdom and method, held together.

how: Vajrayana Buddhists in Tibet, the Himalayas and beyond practice mantra, mandala and visualization, often using a vajra and bell in ritual, and receive practices in person from a teacher through empowerments.

o: a separate religion of Tibet that set the Mahayana aside
the diamond vehicle, Tibet's Buddhism built on the Mahayana
the name of the bell rung in the left hand in Tibetan rites

games.q: you want to take up a Vajrayana practice. a teacher offers you an empowerment tomorrow. what do Tibetan teachers themselves say to do first?
o: accept right away; closeness is the point.
check the teacher carefully, over time.
skip the teacher and learn it from a book.
games.why: because the bond with a teacher is so close and central, Tibetan teachers warn students to check a teacher carefully before trusting.

practice: Think back to your year-one Tibetan weeks: the mantra of Chenrezig, prayer flags in the wind, tonglen, breathing in someone's pain and breathing out relief, Tara who comes quickly, the sand mandala swept away.
Let one of them come back on its own, and stay with it. If it's a mantra, let it sound quietly in your mind; if it's an image, let it sit in front of you.

wordCard.voice: Vajrayana. The diamond vehicle: the Buddhism of Tibet and the Himalayas, built on the Mahayana, with tantra, ritual and a close bond with a teacher. Today's word.

orig.note: Sanskrit: vajrayana, the vajra vehicle. vajra is rendered diamond or thunderbolt; yana is vehicle.

carryVoice: Your line: the diamond vehicle. Wisdom and method, held together. See you tomorrow.
